title: "Thanksgiving Dinner, Measured in Hours of Work"
subtitle: "Prices spiked in 2022. Paychecks caught up. Last year, dinner took the least work in 40 years."
author: "SixtyEight95"
date: "2026-11-18"

---

```{r setup}
source("../../R/fred.R")
source("../../R/thanksgiving_data.R")
library(plotly)
library(knitr)
usd <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2))
hrs <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
```

Every November, the American Farm Bureau Federation shops for the same classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10:
a 16-pound turkey, stuffing, sweet potatoes, rolls, peas, cranberries, a veggie tray, pumpkin pie with whipped
cream, and milk and coffee. They've done it every year since 1986.

The dollar price has roughly doubled since then. But that's only half the story. So, as usual, we asked:
**how long does the average worker have to work to buy it?**

## The short answer

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
In `r tg_latest$year`, the classic dinner for 10 cost **`r usd(tg_latest$cost_for_10)`**. At the average worker's pay, that's
**`r hrs(tg_latest$hours_of_work)` hours of work**, or about **`r round(tg_latest$minutes_per_guest)` minutes per guest.**
That's the least work it has taken in the survey's history. In `r tg_first$year`, it took `r hrs(tg_first$hours_of_work)` hours.
:::

## 40 years of Thanksgiving dinner

```{r hours chart}
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- ggplot(thanksgiving, aes(year, hours_of_work, group = 1,
            text = paste0(year, ": ", usd(cost_for_10), " for 10<br>",
                          hrs(hours_of_work), " hours of work (", round(minutes_per_guest), " min per guest)"))) +
  geom_line(color = "#C05621", linewidth = 0.9) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Hours of work for dinner for 10")
ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

Hover to see the price each year. The dollar cost peaked at **`r usd(tg_peak$cost_for_10)`** in `r tg_peak$year`, when
inflation and bird flu sent turkey prices soaring. That year dinner took `r hrs(tg_peak$hours_of_work)` hours of work, a
visible bump. Since then, the price has fallen three years in a row while pay kept rising, so dinner got easier
to afford on both counts.

## Dollars vs. work

```{r compare table}
thanksgiving %>%
  filter(year %in% c(1986, 1995, 2005, 2015, 2019, 2022, max(year))) %>%
  transmute(Year = year, `Dinner for 10` = usd(cost_for_10), `Average hourly pay` = usd(wage),
            `Hours of work` = hrs(hours_of_work), `Minutes per guest` = round(minutes_per_guest)) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

In dollars, Thanksgiving is about twice as expensive as in 1986. In work time, it's about half the work.

## What about this year?

The Farm Bureau releases its `r tg_latest$year + 1` survey the week before Thanksgiving. We'll update this post when it
comes out. With food prices rising again this fall, we'll be watching to see whether the streak of cheaper
dinners holds.

## The fine print

- **One menu, national average.** The survey prices the same classic menu every year; your actual dinner, store,
  and region will differ. Regional prices in the Northeast and West run well above the national average.
- **A few early years are estimates.** The year-by-year series we used fills a few early gaps using inflation
  data; the Farm Bureau's own figures anchor the start and recent years.
- **Pay is the average worker's hourly earnings in November**, before taxes, for the roughly 80% of private-sector
  workers who aren't managers.

## The bottom line

Thanksgiving dinner feels more expensive because the receipt is bigger. But measured in the time it takes to
earn it, last year's feast was the most affordable in four decades: about **`r round(tg_latest$minutes_per_guest)` minutes
of work per guest.**

---

**How we did this.** Dinner costs are the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual Thanksgiving Dinner Cost
Survey (classic menu for 10). Years 1987–2022 come from a compilation by 24/7 Wall St.; 1986 and 2023–2025 are
from AFBF. Pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees for November of each year,
via [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/AHETPI).
[AFBF survey](https://www.fb.org/market-intel/thanksgiving-dinner-cost-analysis-moderate-decline)
